title: The Good Girl
full_review:
Frustrated by her indolent husband and tedious life, a small-town Texas store clerk has an affair with a brooding young man in the disconcerting story "The Good Girl" (Fox Searchlight).

Those expecting Jennifer Aniston to play a role similar to her perky, fashion-forward Rachel on the TV sitcom "Friends" will be in for a surprise. The role marks a risky departure for Aniston, and she does very well playing against her familiar type.

Aniston plays Justine, a sales clerk in relaxed jeans bored by her life and trapped in a stale marriage with good-natured, pot-smoking house painter, Phil (John C. Reilly). Night after night, Justine comes home to find Phil planted in front of the television set watching cartoons with his dim-witted, sneering buddy Bubba (Tim Blake Nelson). To make things worse, Justine and Phil have been unable to conceive, and the blame has been placed squarely on her. Meanwhile, at her dead-end job at the Retail Rodeo (a low-scale, suburban Kmart-like store), Justine's eyes have begun to wander. The object of her attention is a co-worker, a college drop-out who calls himself Holden (Jake Gyllenhaal) and ponders the meaning of life while flipping through his dog-eared copy of J.D. Salinger's "Catcher in the Rye."

In many ways, "The Good Girl" is a morality play, tinged with wry humor and a nagging conscience that spins into a tale of obsession, betrayal, blackmail, crime and violence. Written by Mike White, who also plays a Retail Rodeo security guard trying to recruit Justine for his Bible study group, the film once again teams up White and director Miguel Areta, whose last venture was the seriously disturbing drama "Chuck & Buck."

"The Good Girl" is a challenging, character-driven black comedy. It represents a more mainstream effort, one which attempts to incorporate the themes of redemption, responsibility and liberation while playing with the audience's willingness to forgive or sympathize with the characters' misguided actions. Yet despite this, the film has several off-putting elements, not least of which is the centerpiece of an extramarital affair.

Justine and Holden find common ground in their mutual hatred of the world. Both feel somehow gypped by life, stuck in jobs and relationships that are beneath their worth. This forms the basis of their association. Justine is flattered to partake in Holden's adolescent-like angst and intrigued by his belief that people just don't "get him" and what's more, they don't get her. For seven years she has been married to a lout, giving up a college education and working a dreary job just to be good. But Holden opens her eyes to the fact that she deserves better. Justine takes a chance on Holden without realizing until too late that she has bounced from one dumb selfish male to another and her life is no better off for it.

As the film progresses, the differences between Holden and Justine become increasingly apparent. Seeing the error of her ways, Justine attempts to right her wrongs. She even takes a stab at journeying on the road to salvation by attending a Bible-study class, only to be confronted by her sin and leave abruptly when she spies the owner of the motel to which she and Holden have been sneaking off. Her attempts aren't exactly successful, but Justine realizes that only she can take responsibility for the way her life is going.

"The Good Girl" is not good for everyone. Probing into the underbelly of selfish human behavior, it offers in return just a glimmer of hope. Justine ends up hurting those around her, but the one sensible decision she does make gives her a second chance at reclaiming her shattered life. Ultimately, "The Good Girl" is a story of unchecked passion which veers off on a serious tangent before righting itself for the film's faux happy ending.

Due to an extramarital affair, a few sexual situations, brief frontal nudity, a suicide, some drug content and sporadic rough language with profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
